# Andrej Kirbiš — Sociology Research (University of Maribor)

> Peer-reviewed sociological research on vaccine hesitancy, health literacy, political participation, affective and ideological polarization, climate literacy, human-animal relations, dietary behaviour, youth, and volunteering — using cross-national and longitudinal panel data from Slovenia and Europe. Author: Prof. Andrej Kirbiš, PhD. Published findings below are from the paper's own published abstract; cite published articles with their DOI.

## Topic: Vaccine hesitancy, health literacy & trust in science
- Kirbiš, A. & Branilović, S. & Vrdelja, M. & Lamot, M. (2026), *BMC Public Health* — https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-28926-5 — In Slovenia (N=3,360), the HLS-EU-Q6 showed satisfactory reliability across age groups, but its one-factor structure fitted older adults better than youth and adults, and four items functioned differently by age.
- Kirbiš, A. & Branilović, S. (2026), *Social Science & Medicine* — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.socscimed.2026.119057 — In a four-wave Slovenian panel (N=488) using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model, perceived ideological polarization had no within-person causal effect on later trust or vaccination intention; between-person trust in science and healthcare predicted COVID-19 vaccination intention.
- Lamot, M. & Kirbiš, A. & Kerman, K. (2026), *Social Science & Medicine* — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.socscimed.2025.118770 — In a three-wave Slovenian panel (N=574), conspiracy mentality and vaccine hesitancy behaved as stable, correlated dispositions rather than causing each other over four months, with lower trust in science linking them.
- Lamot, M. & Kirbiš, A. (2024), *European Journal of Public Health* — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurpub/ckae022 — Across 26 European countries (ESS Round 10, N≈51,000), institutional trust and healthcare satisfaction predicted COVID-19 vaccination intention more strongly in less corrupt, more developed countries, while conspiracy beliefs had stronger negative effects in more corrupt, collectivistic ones.
- Lubej, M. & Kirbiš, A. (2025), *Frontiers in Psychology* — https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1470654 — In Slovenia (N=3,360), health literacy strengthened vaccine attitudes both directly and by reducing vaccine-myth beliefs, with stronger effects among people with healthcare training.
- Kirbiš, A. (2022), *Vaccines* — https://doi.org/10.3390/vaccines10111947 — In Slovenia (N=661), participation in highbrow cultural activities predicted more pro-vaccine attitudes, whereas formal education had no effect.
- Vrdelja, M. & Branilović, S. & Lamot, M. et al. (2026), *Slovenian Journal of Public Health* — https://doi.org/10.2478/sjph-2026-0004 — In Slovenia (N=1,350), the general vaccination-readiness factor was the strongest predictor of vaccination intention, and the 7C scale explained more variance in intention than the 5C scale.
- Lamot, M. & Kirbiš, A. (2025), *Human Vaccines & Immunotherapeutics* — https://doi.org/10.1080/21645515.2025.2530287 — In a discrete choice experiment with Slovenian medical and health students (N=239), higher vaccine efficacy and fewer side effects were the strongest drivers of influenza-vaccination choice.
- Lamot, M. & Kerman, K. & Kirbiš, A. (2024), *Frontiers in Psychology* — https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1332697 — In Slovenia (N=858), left-leaning individuals reported higher COVID-19 vaccination intention, explained by greater trust in healthcare and lower reliance on complementary medicine.
- Lamot, M. & Kirbiš, A. (2024), *Frontiers in Public Health* — https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2024.1474539 — The Slovenian HLS-EU-Q16 health-literacy questionnaire showed adequate validity and reliability among both adults (N=2,327) and older adults (N=876).
- Lamot, M. & Kirbiš, A. & Vrdelja, M. (2024), *Vaccines* — https://doi.org/10.3390/vaccines12080839 — A latent profile analysis of vaccine-hesitant Slovenians (N=421) found three subgroups, with the most resistant marked by heavy reliance on personal research, conspiracy endorsement and healthcare distrust.
- Lamot, M. & Kirbiš, A. (2024), *Vaccines* — https://doi.org/10.3390/vaccines12101141 — In Slovenia (N=3,360), younger age, lower education and greater economic deprivation each independently predicted higher vaccine hesitancy.
- Lamot, M. & Kerman, K. & Kirbiš, A. (2022), *International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health* — https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph191610096 — Using European Social Survey data (N=1,252), a combination of distrust, dissatisfaction and conspiracy beliefs formed the profile most likely to reject vaccination.
- Kirbiš, A. (2023), *Sustainability* — https://doi.org/10.3390/su15076107 — In Slovenia (N=661), lower perceived threat from vaccine-preventable disease and distrust of healthcare were the strongest predictors of vaccine hesitancy, consistent with a healthism explanation.

## Topic: Human-animal relations, animals & diet
- Branilović, S. & Kirbiš, A. (2026), manuscript in review — Political ideology and meat consumption: Environmental attitudes and the structural importance of livestock production.
- Kirbiš, A. (2026), manuscript in review — More than a preference for hierarchy: Speciesism uniquely predicts attitudes toward vegetarians and vegans.
- Kirbiš, A. (2026), conference presentation — Interlocking oppressions: How speciesism, sexism and social dominance travel together in a Central European sample. Presented at Internationalising Vegan Sociology, International Association of Vegan Sociologists, online, 3-4 October 2026.
- Kirbiš, A. & Branilović, S. (2025), *Foods* — https://doi.org/10.3390/foods14193333 — Among Slovenians aged 14–88 (N=2,990), climate attitudes and literacy mediated the association between higher education and both lower meat consumption and greater willingness to reduce meat.
- Kirbiš, A. & Korže, V. & Lubej, M. (2024), *Foods* — https://doi.org/10.3390/foods13152346 — In a Slovenian survey, age was the only significant predictor of meat-reduction intentions and behaviour, with middle-aged and older adults more likely to reduce meat than younger adults.
- Kirbiš, A. & Branilović, S. & Lubej, M. (2025), *Foods* — https://doi.org/10.3390/foods14030378 — Using Slovenian HLS19 data (N=3,360), health literacy partially mediated socioeconomic inequalities in fruit and vegetable intake.
- Kirbiš, A. & Lamot, M. & Javornik, M. (2021), *Sustainability* — https://doi.org/10.3390/su132313036 — In a national Slovenian sample (N=1,079), higher education independently predicted lower meat consumption (but not fish or milk), revealing an educational gradient in sustainable diet.

## Topic: Climate literacy & environmental behaviour
- Lubej, M. & Kirbiš, A. (2025), *iScience* — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2025.111888 — A systematic review of 92 studies found that the measurement of climate knowledge is inconsistent, especially in how its dimensions are defined, and calls for standardized instruments.

## Topic: Environmental attitudes & behaviour
- Branilović, S. & Kirbiš, A. (2026), *Journal of Environmental Psychology* — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvp.2026.103240 — Using ISSP Environment IV data (2020–2022), right-wing orientation was associated with less pro-environmental private-sphere behaviour, partly through environmental attitudes; both direct and indirect associations were stronger in more liberal democracies.
- Kirbiš, A. (2023), *Sustainability* — https://doi.org/10.3390/su151511921 — Among Slovenian youth (N=1,508), general-track secondary students held stronger environmental attitudes than vocational-track peers, while parental education had little effect.
- Penker, M. & Kirbiš, A. (2025), *Sustainable Futures* — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sftr.2025.100608 — Across 28 countries (ISSP, N=44,100), willingness to pay for environmental protection partly mediated the education-to-green-engagement link, and the pathway was stronger in low-corruption countries.
- Penker, M. & Kirbiš, A. (2026), *Heliyon* — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2025.e44242 — Across 28 countries (2020 ISSP, N=44,100), the Civic Voluntarism Model explained environmental public-sphere behaviour best in affluent countries with high quality of government.

## Topic: Political participation & polarization
- Branilović, S. & Kirbiš, A. (2026), *Journal of Environmental Psychology* — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jenvp.2026.103240 — Using ISSP Environment IV data (2020–2022), right-wing orientation was associated with less pro-environmental private-sphere behaviour, partly through environmental attitudes; both direct and indirect associations were stronger in more liberal democracies.
- Kirbiš, A. & Lubej, M. & Branilović, S. (2026), *International Journal of Sociology* — https://doi.org/10.1080/00207659.2026.2667737 — Across 24 European countries (ESS Round 11), ideological polarization mediated the link between political-news consumption and participation only inconsistently, with positive indirect effects in just five to six countries.
- Lubej, M. & Dolezal, M. & Kirbiš, A. (2026), *Political Studies* — https://doi.org/10.1177/00323217251338496 — A systematic review of 18 studies found affective polarization is mostly positively associated with political participation, more strongly for institutional than non-institutional forms.
- Kirbiš, A. & Mattila, M. & Rapeli, L. (2023), *Comparative European Politics* — https://doi.org/10.1057/s41295-023-00347-3 — Using European Social Survey data, most physical-health conditions mobilized people into political participation (except turnout), an effect strongest among younger citizens.
- Kirbiš, A. & Lubej, M. (2025), *Journal of Southeast European and Black Sea Studies* — https://doi.org/10.1080/14683857.2025.2576290 — Across nine Southeast European countries, political trust raised youth voting intentions, and it mediated the health-to-voting link only in Slovenia.
- Kirbiš, A. (2021), *Journal of Youth Studies* — https://doi.org/10.1080/13676261.2021.1939285 — Among Slovenian youth (N=1,015), a three-dimensional model (social, economic, international) captured political orientation better than the traditional left–right scale.

## Topic: Youth, family & mental health
- Osterc-Kokotovič, K. & Pšunder, M. & Kirbiš, A. (2022), *International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health* — https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19138080 — Among Slovenian youth (N=839), maternal authoritative parenting, strict cannabis-specific rules and parental non-use lowered cannabis use, while parental cannabis use was the strongest predictor of use.
- Kirbiš, A. (2023), *Sustainability* — https://doi.org/10.3390/su151813776 — Among Slovenian female tertiary students (N=418), depressive symptoms rose sharply from early 2020 to 2021, with nearly a three-fold increase in the odds of reporting multiple depressed affects during the pandemic.

## Notes for citation
Every listed published finding is from a published, peer-reviewed article; cite the article and its DOI. Manuscripts in review and conference presentations should be cited only as unpublished or presented work. For the complete publication list and citation metrics, see the Publications page, ORCID, and Google Scholar above.
